title: How Tour Operators Book Gorilla Permits for Clients in Uganda and Rwanda
meta_title: Gorilla Permits for Tour Operators in Uganda and Rwanda
meta_description: Gorilla permits for tour operators in Uganda and Rwanda: who can book, prices, deposits, rescheduling fees and the client details to collect first.
excerpt: A practical guide to gorilla permits for tour operators and travel agents: how UWA and RDB sell permits, what they cost, deposit and rescheduling rules, and what to collect from clients.
content:
Gorilla permits for tour operators are bought from two government bodies: the Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA), which sells Bwindi and Mgahinga permits to foreign visitors only through licensed operators, and the Rwanda Development Board (RDB), whose portal lets licensed agents hold Volcanoes National Park permits with a deposit. Prices are fixed by each tariff, with no trade discount.

For an overseas agent the difficulty is not the price but the paperwork around it: who is allowed to buy, what you must collect from clients, when the money is due and what happens when someone falls ill. This guide walks through gorilla permits for tour operators step by step for both countries, in the order a booking really happens. It is the process our safari DMC service for travel agents and tour leaders follows from Nairobi when partners send us gorilla requests.

Quick Facts

  • Uganda seller: Uganda Wildlife Authority; foreign non-residents can only book through tour operators licensed by the Uganda Tourism Board
  • Rwanda seller: Rwanda Development Board, through its online booking portal
  • Uganda permit: US$800 per foreign non-resident, US$600 in April, May and November (January 2027 to June 2028 tariff, checked November 2026)
  • Rwanda permit: US$1,500 per foreign non-resident (checked October 2026)
  • Rwanda advance booking: Operators can hold a permit with a 40-99% deposit and pay the balance before 30 days to the trek
  • Group and age limits: Up to 8 visitors per gorilla family for one hour; trekkers must be 15 or older
  • Rescheduling: Uganda charges 25% of the permit fee for late changes; a confirmed Rwanda permit costs 20% to move

Who Is Allowed to Book Gorilla Permits in Uganda and Rwanda?

Gorilla permits for tour operators work differently in each country. In Uganda, foreign non-residents and residents of other African countries can only buy gorilla and chimpanzee permits through tour operators licensed by the Uganda Tourism Board. In Rwanda, travellers can buy direct, but licensed agents get extra booking tools.

This matters for overseas agents because a travel agency in London, Frankfurt or Toronto is not on either country's licensed list. In practice, gorilla permits for tour operators abroad are bought by a local licensed company in its own account, which then issues each permit in your client's name and carries the risk on the ground. Choosing that partner is the first decision, and our guide to what an East Africa DMC does for overseas agents covers the wider relationship.

Uganda: licensed operators only

The Uganda Wildlife Authority states in its conservation tariff for January 2027 to June 2028 that gorilla and chimpanzee permits for foreign non-residents and residents of other African countries can only be booked through licensed tour operators. UWA introduced an online booking system for licensed operators in 2024, with permits checked by QR code at the park. Since a January 2026 directive, UWA no longer hands paper permits to operators: the operator pays, receives an official receipt, and the permit is sent electronically to the operator's official email address.

Rwanda: direct sales plus agent tools

The Rwanda Development Board sells permits to anyone through its booking portal, so an independent traveller can buy one with a card. The difference for gorilla permits for tour operators is the advance booking service, which lets a registered tour operator hold a date with a part payment, and a separate rescheduling service for those deposit bookings. Both are described below.

Gorilla Permit Prices to Build Into Client Quotes

Gorilla permits for tour operators cost exactly what independent travellers pay: prices are set by the national authorities and published in their tariffs, with no separate trade rate. A foreign non-resident pays US$800 in Uganda and US$1,500 in Rwanda, and a good local partner itemises it at cost.

Permit and visitor categoryUganda (Bwindi, Mgahinga)Rwanda (Volcanoes)
Gorilla trek, foreign non-residentUS$800US$1,500
Low-season rate, foreign non-residentUS$600 in April, May and NovemberUS$1,050 (30% off) November to May with two nights in Akagera or Nyungwe
Gorilla trek, foreign residentUS$700 (US$500 in the low months)US$500 promotional rate for African residents
Other African citizensUS$500US$500 promotional rate
Gorilla habituation, foreign non-residentUS$1,800Not offered

Uganda figures come from the UWA tariff for January 2027 to June 2028 (checked November 2026); Rwanda figures from RDB pages and its January 2026 rate announcement (checked October 2026). Rwanda had not published 2027 rates when we checked, so anyone quoting gorilla permits for tour operators' 2027 programmes should confirm every rate before it goes into a client contract.

What the permit price includes

The Uganda permit includes the ranger guide, that day's park entrance and a community contribution. Porters, lodge nights, transport and tips sit outside the permit. For the full traveller-facing picture, our Rwanda gorilla permit guide explains the discounts and resident rules client by client.

How Does a Gorilla Permit Booking Work, Step by Step?

When we buy gorilla permits for tour operators, the booking runs in the same order in both countries: confirm the date and gorilla family availability, collect each client's passport details, pay the authority, then receive the permit in the client's name. Uganda expects payment upfront; Rwanda lets operators hold a date with a deposit.

Gorilla permits for tour operators in Uganda

  1. Check availability by sector: Bwindi has four trekking sectors (Buhoma, Ruhija, Rushaga and Nkuringo), each with its own gorilla families, plus Mgahinga to the south.
  2. Collect client details: full name as in the passport, nationality and passport number for every trekker.
  3. Pay UWA: by bank transfer or the online payment portal; the tariff also lists mobile money and card machines.
  4. Receive the receipt and permit: the receipt comes first, then the permit arrives by email to the operator's official address.
  5. Book the lodge in the same sector: a Rushaga permit with a Buhoma lodge can mean a very early drive of two hours or more.

Our Bwindi gorilla trekking guide compares the four sectors, useful background for anyone handling gorilla permits for tour operators in Uganda when a client asks for an easier walk or a particular lodge.

Rwanda's advance booking with deposit

The RDB advance booking page for tour operators lets an operator reserve a permit by paying between 40% and 99% of the fee, then confirm it by paying the balance before 30 days to the visit date (checked November 2026). Confirmation uses the booking reference number, and RDB does not allow cash payment at the park. This is how operators hold gorilla permits for tour operators' group departures while the rest of the itinerary is still being agreed.

The deposit route suits early enquiries, but it creates a hard deadline. If the balance is not paid in time, the operator risks losing the slot, so build the 30-day cut-off into your own client payment schedule, as our post on how safari net rates and deposits work for travel agents explains.

Rescheduling and Cancelling Gorilla Permits for Tour Operators

Gorilla permits for tour operators are effectively non-refundable in both countries, but each authority allows paid changes. Uganda charges 25% of the permit fee for late rescheduling and 50% to trek in a different location. Rwanda charges 20% to move a confirmed permit and offers free date changes on deposit bookings made at least 30 days ahead.

SituationUganda (UWA)Rwanda (RDB)
Change the trek date25% of the permit fee for late rescheduling20% of the fee on a confirmed permit; requests more than 7 days ahead are approved automatically
Move a deposit bookingNot applicableNo fee if requested 30 days or more before the visit; otherwise the permit expires
Trek in another sector or park50% of the permit feeOne park only (Volcanoes)
Change the travellerPermits are non-transferable; ask UWA through your operatorThe portal lists a permit transfer service; the fee depends on the permit type
No-show on the dayNo refund stated in the tariffThe permit is treated as expired

Rwanda's fees come from the RDB portal (checked October and November 2026) and Uganda's from the UWA tariff (checked November 2026). Both authorities also tell visitors not to trek with a cold or other infectious illness, because gorillas catch human diseases. Neither publishes a refund for illness, so your client terms should say clearly who absorbs the cost if a traveller is turned back at the briefing.

Mirror the rules in your own terms

When we arrange gorilla permits for tour operators, we suggest passing the authority's rules straight through to the client: the permit is paid in full and non-refundable once bought, changes cost what the authority charges, and the client must carry travel insurance that covers non-refundable activities. Our travel insurance page lists the cover we suggest to partners' clients.

What Should You Collect From Clients Before Buying Permits?

Before we buy gorilla permits for tour operators, we need each trekker's full name exactly as in the passport, nationality, passport number and date of birth, plus proof of residence for anyone claiming a resident rate. Collect it at deposit stage, because permits are issued in each trekker's name and changes cost money.

Check ages too. The minimum age for gorilla trekking is 15 in both Uganda and Rwanda, and rangers can ask for proof at the briefing, so a family with a 14-year-old needs a different plan. Ask about fitness honestly: treks can take from under an hour to most of a day on steep, muddy slopes, and porters and walking sticks help. Our article on how hard gorilla trekking is is a useful link to send clients before they commit.

Groups larger than eight

Large groups are where gorilla permits for tour operators get complicated. Each habituated gorilla family takes a maximum of eight visitors a day, so a party of 12 needs permits for two families on the same date, and they will trek separately. For larger parties, check how many families one sector can offer before quoting. Our guide to group gorilla trekking in Uganda sets out how many families different group sizes need, and our group safaris team handles clubs, schools and incentive groups.

Uganda or Rwanda: Which Permit Suits Your Client?

Uganda suits clients who want a lower permit price, a longer stay and the option of the four-hour habituation experience. Rwanda suits clients short on time, because Volcanoes National Park is roughly a two to three hour drive from Kigali and a gorilla trek fits into a three or four day trip.

The permit gap is large: at standard rates a Rwanda trek costs US$700 more per person than a Bwindi trek, so for a group of eight that is US$5,600 before anything else. Against that, Bwindi is a long drive or a domestic flight from Entebbe, which adds nights and transport. Ready-made examples help when you pitch either option: our 4 day gorilla trekking safari to Bwindi is a private road trip from Entebbe, and the 4 day Rwanda double gorilla trekking safari gives keen clients two treks with two different families. For a deeper look at the two parks, see our Bwindi vs Volcanoes comparison.

When to book

Timing is the biggest risk with gorilla permits for tour operators: book as soon as dates are fixed. The dry months of June to September and December to February sell out first, and many operators aim for six months or more ahead for those dates. The Uganda low-season rate in April, May and November and Rwanda's November to May discount make the wetter months worth offering to price-sensitive clients.

Insider Tips

  • Permits before flights: Confirm the permit date, then book lodges and international flights around it
  • Names at deposit: Collect passport names, nationalities and dates of birth when the client pays the deposit, not at final payment
  • Itemise permits: Show permits as a separate line at cost so clients see where the money goes and why it is non-refundable
  • Diary the Rwanda cut-off: Advance bookings must be confirmed or moved before 30 days to the trek
  • Match sector and lodge: In Bwindi, book the lodge in the same sector as the permit
  • Plan the under-15s: Arrange a community walk, golden monkeys or a lodge day for younger family members

Frequently Asked Questions

Can overseas travel agents book gorilla permits directly?

Overseas travel agents cannot book Uganda gorilla permits directly, because UWA sells them to foreign non-residents only through operators licensed by the Uganda Tourism Board. Anyone can buy Rwanda permits on the RDB portal, but advance booking with a deposit is for registered operators, so most agents use a licensed local partner.

How far ahead should tour operators book gorilla permits?

Gorilla permits for tour operators should be booked as soon as a client's dates are fixed, and six months or more ahead for June to September and December to February, when permits sell out first. Rwanda's advance booking lets an operator hold a date with a deposit of 40% to 99%, with the balance due before 30 days to the trek.

Are gorilla permits refundable if a client cancels?

Gorilla permits are generally not refundable in Uganda or Rwanda once bought, though both authorities allow paid changes. Uganda charges 25% of the permit fee for late rescheduling, and Rwanda charges 20% to move a confirmed permit. A no-show means the permit is lost, so clients need insurance that covers non-refundable activity costs.

Do gorilla permits for tour operators include a commission?

Gorilla permits for tour operators carry no built-in commission or trade discount, because the Uganda Wildlife Authority and the Rwanda Development Board publish one price per visitor category. Local partners normally pass the permit through at cost as an itemised line, and agents decide whether to add a small markup to cover payment and handling costs.

What client details are needed for a gorilla permit?

A gorilla permit needs each trekker's full name exactly as in the passport, nationality and passport number, and operators usually ask for date of birth to confirm the minimum age of 15. Anyone claiming a resident or East African rate must show proof of status, which rangers can check at the briefing.

Final Thoughts

Gorilla permits for tour operators come down to three things: buy through a licensed local partner, collect passport details early, and pass the authorities' payment and change rules straight to your clients. Get those right and the permit stops being the risky part of the trip.
